common_name: Silver Shimmers Lungwort (Large Solid-Silver Leaf Pulmonaria)

planting.note: Plant divisions in early spring or early fall in consistently moist, humus-rich soil with good air movement; site where afternoon shade protects the heavily silvered leaves from scorch.

directions: This selection carries unusually long, undulating leaves that read almost entirely solid silver, with only a thin ruffled edge of green tracing the margin, making it one of the most dramatically pale-leaved lungworts available. Pink buds open in very early spring to large cobalt-blue flowers held just above the foliage, among the biggest blooms in the genus. The clump stays low and mounded, gradually widening into a dense, shimmering groundcover under deciduous shade. Keep soil evenly moist and provide good airflow, since dense foliage and heat stress can invite mildew in muggy climates.

common_name: Smoky Blue Lungwort (Cream-Spotted Foliage with Smoky-Blue Flowers)

planting.note: Divide and plant in spring or early fall into fertile, humus-rich, evenly moist soil; useful beneath deciduous trees and shrubs where it tolerates root competition and dry shade once established.

directions: A spreading, clump-forming lungwort with ovate dark-green leaves speckled in cream, this cultivar opens pink flower buds in early spring that quickly shift to a dusky, smoky blue as they mature, giving the clusters a two-toned look. Bloom is concentrated in April and May, ahead of most other shade perennials, after which the speckled foliage remains an attractive groundcover through the growing season. It tolerates deeper shade and drier soil than many lungworts once settled in, though it still performs best with consistent moisture. Shear tired summer foliage back hard if it declines, and it will reflush with cleaner new leaves.

planting.note: Plant divisions in early spring or fall in cool, humusy, evenly moist but well-drained soil; semi-evergreen foliage benefits from a sheltered spot where winter leaves can persist.

directions: A vigorous, semi-evergreen selection that arose as a garden seedling in England, this cultivar bears broad, dark-green leaves so heavily overlaid with silvery-white spotting that the pattern reads as bold and almost continuous rather than finely flecked. Reddish-pink flowers fading toward lavender-blue open from March into April, held in coiled clusters typical of the genus. The dark foliage backdrop makes the silver markings especially prominent, and the semi-evergreen habit keeps the clump looking presentable through much of winter in milder climates. Grow in consistently moist, rich soil in part to full shade, and divide every few years to maintain vigor and foliage quality.

common_name: Ann Red Lungwort (Early-Blooming Unspotted Pale-Green Foliage)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in part to full shade; spreads slowly by creeping roots and works well as a woodland-edge groundcover.

directions: This selection of red lungwort carries pale-green, unspotted, bristly leaves typical of the species, forming a soft-textured semi-evergreen mound. Flowers open in late winter into early spring in two-toned clusters of red with pale white margins, giving an unusually bicolor effect compared with the solid coral-red of the straight species. Bloom is among the earliest of any lungwort, often appearing while little else is active in the shade bed. It spreads gradually by creeping roots to form a modest, non-invasive patch and tolerates heavier shade and root competition from nearby trees better than many hybrid lungworts.

common_name: Coral Springs Lungwort (Narrow Silver-Speckled Leaves, Coral-Pink Flowers)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall into cool, organically rich, consistently moist soil; a good edging or path-side plant where its unusual flower color can be appreciated up close.

directions: This cultivar carries narrow, silver-speckled leaves similar in pattern to older narrow-leaved lungwort selections, but breaks from the typical blue flower palette with an abundance of coral-pink blooms in early spring instead of the usual pink-to-blue progression. The narrow foliage gives the clump a finer, more delicate texture than broad-leaved saccharata types, and it spreads at a moderate pace to form a loose, airy groundcover. Grow in average to rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in part to full shade, and avoid letting it dry out during summer to keep foliage from scorching.

common_name: Baby Blue Lungwort (Compact Tight-Mounding Silver-Spotted Pulmonaria)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, humus-rich soil; its small, tidy habit suits edging, small beds, or container plantings in shade where larger lungworts would overwhelm the space.

directions: One of the most compact lungworts available, this selection forms a small, tight, evenly mounded clump of silver-spotted foliage that resists the open, splitting-center habit common to older cultivars as it matures. In early spring the mound is smothered in flowers that open pink and age to a soft baby blue, creating a dense wash of color proportionally large for such a small plant. Its diminutive size makes it well suited to small shade gardens, rock garden edges, or containers where full-size lungworts would crowd out neighbors. Keep soil evenly moist through summer and provide good air circulation to discourage powdery mildew.

common_name: Starry Eyes Siberian Bugloss (Bicolor Blue-Edged White Star Flowers)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich garden soil in part shade; tolerates drier shade once established beneath deciduous trees and shrubs.

directions: This cultivar stands apart from the typical all-blue Siberian bugloss by producing small, star-shaped flowers that are white at the center with a distinct edging of bright gentian blue around each petal, an unusual bicolor effect in the genus. The sprays of starry blooms rise above mounds of heart-shaped, mid-green leaves in mid-spring, and plants quickly form a dense, weed-suppressing clump. It performs reliably in cool or even dry shade once established and makes an effective groundcover beneath deciduous trees and shrubs. Divide congested clumps in early fall every few years to maintain vigor and flower display.

common_name: Pirate's Patch Foamflower (Black-Centered Fuzzy Green Leaves)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in part to full shade; a good choice for edging shaded paths and woodland borders.

directions: Each fuzzy, lobed green leaf on this selection carries a bold dark-centered patch radiating out from the midrib, giving the low, dense foliage mound a distinctive patterned look even before bloom. In late spring the clump sends up abundant slender spikes of small white flowers well above the leaves, producing a frothy, airy display over the patterned foliage. Foliage takes on good bronze tones in fall and is evergreen to semi-evergreen in milder climates, giving the planting multi-season interest. Grow in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in part to full shade, where it works well as a dense, low edging plant along shaded paths.

common_name: Dark Star Foamflower (Star-Shaped Maple-Like Leaves with Burgundy Center)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall into moist, humus-rich soil in part shade to light shade; spreads slowly by stolons into a wider patch over time.

directions: This selection forms a mound of unusual star-shaped, deeply lobed, maple-like leaves marked with a dark burgundy center that intensifies as the season progresses. Foliage emerges chartreuse in spring, deepens to dark green with contrasting burgundy veining through summer, and often turns coppery bronze in fall, giving the planting color interest well beyond its bloom period. In early spring the mound is topped with short, dense spikes of white bottle-brush flowers held just above the leaves. It spreads gradually by stolons to form a slowly widening patch, making it useful as a textured groundcover at the front of a shaded border.
